name: Pretraining data
summary: The huge collection of text and other media a model first learns from, and how it is filtered.

text: Before an AI can talk, it reads an enormous amount: websites, books and code. It's like a child who has read a whole library.
People try to remove junk and repeated pages first, because the AI learns whatever it reads.
D1.analogy: A child who has read an entire library, including the junk mail.

text: Pretraining corpora are assembled from sources such as web crawls, code repositories, books and papers, then filtered.
Typical steps: extract the text, remove duplicates, filter low-quality or harmful content, detect language, and remove personal data where possible.
Quality matters as much as quantity: better-curated data can rival much larger, noisier datasets.

diagram.caption: From the web to training tokens

D2.analogy: Like panning for gold: most of what you scoop up is gravel.
D2.analogyBreaks: Gold either is gold or isn't. With data, 'quality' is a judgement call, and filters can remove useful dialects or topics along with the junk.

predict.question: A web crawl contains the same article copied thousands of times. What's the main risk of training on it unchanged?
options: The model over-weights it and may memorise it word for word
predict.explanation: Duplicates skew what the model learns and increase verbatim memorisation, which is why deduplication is standard.

text: Open questions: the limited supply of high-quality human text, licensing and consent, measuring data quality, and benchmark questions leaking into training data (contamination).

sources.title: The FineWeb Datasets: Decanting the Web for the Finest Text Data at Scale
